title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect for APIs
hook: OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization — who may access what on whose behalf. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity on top with standard login and ID tokens. Your API usually validates access tokens, not the user's password.

blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework: clients obtain access tokens from an authorization server to call resource servers (your Web API). OpenID Connect extends OAuth with an identity layer — ID token (JWT) proves who logged in; access token authorizes API calls. ASP.NET Core APIs typically use JwtBearer with Authority pointing at the OIDC metadata document (.well-known/openid-configuration) to fetch signing keys and issuer. Interactive login flows (authorization code + PKCE) happen in the browser or BFF — not inside a pure JSON API controller.

entries.plainDefinition: Protocol for delegated access via access tokens without sharing user passwords with third-party apps.
entries.example: Mobile app calls API with token from Auth0

entries.plainDefinition: Identity layer on OAuth — ID token, UserInfo endpoint, standard claims (sub, email).
Issues tokens — Entra ID, Auth0, IdentityServer, Keycloak.
Extension securing authorization code flow for public clients (SPAs, mobile) without client secret.

blocks.text: Building custom username/password login in every API duplicates security bugs. Standard OAuth/OIDC flows give refresh rotation, MFA at the IdP, and centralized revocation. Senior interviews ask which grant types are allowed today (authorization code + PKCE; avoid implicit and password grant), what the API validates (access token aud/scope, not ID token for API auth), and how service-to-service uses client credentials.

blocks.title: API validates access token
blocks.body: ID token is for the client to know who signed in. Resource APIs should validate the access token's audience and scopes — unless your API is the OIDC userinfo endpoint itself.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Authorize redirect
items.body: Client redirects user to IdP /authorize with client_id, scope, redirect_uri, code_challenge.

items.title: User authenticates at IdP
items.body: MFA, password, federated login — all at the trusted authorization server.

items.title: Code exchanged for tokens
items.body: Client POSTs to /token with code + code_verifier → access_token, refresh_token, id_token.

items.title: API call
items.body: Client sends access_token as Bearer; API validates via JwtBearer Authority metadata.

diagram.title: OAuth 2.0 actors for a Web API
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  User[Resource Owner] --> Client[Client SPA or Mobile]
  Client -->|1 authorize + PKCE| AS[Authorization Server\nOIDC]
  AS -->|2 tokens| Client
  Client -->|3 Bearer access_token| API[Resource Server\nASP.NET Core API]
  API -->|4 validate JWT metadata| AS

snippet.label: API trusts Entra ID / generic OIDC Authority
snippet.explanation: Authority loads OIDC metadata and JWKS automatically. Audience must match app registration API identifier. Scope claims differ by IdP — know your token shape.

snippet.label: Client credentials (service-to-service)
snippet.explanation: Client credentials grant has no user sub claim — policies must use scopes or app roles, not user ownership defaults.

snippet.label: BFF pattern — OIDC cookie for browser, JWT for API
snippet.explanation: Browser apps use OIDC middleware on the BFF; JavaScript calls same-origin BFF which attaches Bearer token server-side.

snippet.label: Diagnostic — log metadata refresh failures
snippet.explanation: After IdP key rotation, APIs fail all tokens until ConfigurationManager refreshes JWKS — monitor this exception in production.

blocks.title: OIDC client libraries vs ASP.NET Core
rows: OpenIdConnect middleware on BFF, not API
SaveTokens in cookie session on server
RequireClaim on scp or scope claim

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using resource owner password grant in new apps. Validating ID token at the API instead of access token. Missing PKCE on public clients. Hard-coding JWKS keys instead of metadata refresh. Treating client_credentials tokens like user tokens in ownership checks.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: correlate 401 spikes with IdP deployment or certificate rotation timestamps. Use token introspection (RFC 7662) for opaque tokens or high-security immediate revocation. Document which grant types each client uses — security audits flag password and implicit grants. OpenTelemetry baggage propagating sub and tenant from validated access token aids cross-service tracing without re-parsing JWT in every service manually.

blocks.title: Grant type suitability (2024+ guidance)
rows: Phishing, no MFA at IdP UX

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain difference between ID token and access token. Recommending implicit flow for SPAs. Saying API should accept username/password POST to /login in OAuth architecture. Not knowing PKCE purpose.

interviewTakeaways: OAuth 2.0 = delegated access tokens; OIDC adds identity (ID token, metadata, standard claims).
APIs validate access token audience/scopes via JwtBearer Authority — not ID token for resource access.
Production tip: monitor JWKS refresh failures; use authorization code + PKCE; rotate refresh tokens.
60s: User logs in at IdP via code+PKCE. Client gets access and refresh tokens. API validates JWT against OIDC metadata. BFF keeps refresh HttpOnly. Client credentials for machine-to-machine.
Follow-up: how does token introspection differ from local JWT validation?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'use ID token to call API' gets you rejected — access token is for resource server; ID token is for client identity.
Password grant for new mobile apps — OAuth working group deprecates it; use authorization code + PKCE.
Strong answer: 'Separate authorization server from API. API is resource server validating aud and scp. Browser uses BFF; mobile uses PKCE; services use client credentials.'
introducedIn: AddOpenIdConnect in ASP.NET Core 1.0; PKCE support in 2.1+

jsTsCorrelations.note: signinRedirect + PKCE parallels OpenIdConnect middleware UsePkce on BFF — tokens never handled identically but flow matches.
Guard validates JWT same as JwtBearer; scope decorators map to RequireClaim on scp — IdP-specific claim names still apply.
